implementation_notes: Stage one builds the logical page as a DOM tree with domain element names. Stage two compiles each channel's stylesheet once into a Templates and obtains a Transformer per render; the javadoc states plainly that a Transformer may not be used by several threads at once, so the compiled Templates is the shared artefact and the Transformer is request state. transform(Source, Result) writes to a StreamResult over a Writer, a file or a response, which keeps renderer tests free of a servlet container. Choose it when one logical page must be published as HTML and as a styled, machine-readable XML or PDF artefact; for ordinary request-scoped web pages the Spring variant is usually the better fit.
pitfalls: A Transformer must not be shared between threads (javadoc), so caching the Transformer instead of the Templates corrupts output under load.
The default DocumentBuilderFactory and TransformerFactory resolve external entities and allow document()/import, so harden both when the page or the stylesheet can be influenced from outside.
Materialising the whole page as DOM costs memory proportional to the page; very large pages must be streamed, which is Transform View rather than this pattern.

variants.name: Spring MVC model + ViewResolver / ContentNegotiatingViewResolver
variants.idiom_name: ModelAndView + ViewResolver chain with one View per representation
variants.implementation_notes: The controller returns a model plus a logical view name (ModelAndView), and the ViewResolver chain maps that name to a View; the View is the renderer - Thymeleaf or JSP for HTML, a Jackson-backed JSON view for JSON, a marshalling view for XML, a PDF view for print. Spring documents ContentNegotiatingViewResolver as choosing the representation from the Accept header or a format parameter by comparing media types against the View content types, which is the channel resolver of the pattern. Choose this variant when a servlet container and Spring are already in the stack; keep the model free of view-technology types and view names in one place, because a logical view name is a string contract resolved at request time.
pitfalls: The logical view name is resolved at request time, so a typo renders the wrong template or fails at runtime - keep the names in one place and assert them in tests.
A model exposing JPA entities with lazy associations invites the renderer to trigger queries mid-render (LazyInitializationException in the view layer).
ViewResolver chains are order-sensitive: InternalResourceViewResolver cannot report a missing JSP without dispatching, so it must come last.
